lines.text: Build a real, fixed-size page as its own byte buffer, with its own header baked right into those bytes: a magic number, a version, a checksum, a log position.
Now flip one byte somewhere in that page's body, on purpose. Does the page notice, or does it just hand back the wrong data without complaint?
It notices.
The page's own checksum catches it, wherever that flipped byte happens to land.
Run it for real: an untouched page's checksum validates cleanly on its own.
Flip a single byte anywhere in that same page, and the checksum genuinely stops validating, with nothing outside the page telling it where to look.
Instead of corrupting a byte, change the page's own magic number to something else entirely, then recompute the checksum over those new bytes, honestly, the same way the page always does.
Does the checksum alone catch that the format itself has quietly changed underneath it?
No, it doesn't.
A checksum recomputed over consistent new bytes still validates; it was never built to notice a deliberate, consistent change.
Run it for real: with the magic number changed and the checksum honestly recomputed over the new bytes, that checksum still validates cleanly.
Only checking the magic number itself caught that the format had actually changed.
The page's own multi-byte fields, like its log position, are written out in a specific byte order, chosen on purpose and never left to chance.
Take those exact same raw bytes and read them back in the opposite order instead.
Does that choice actually matter, or is one byte order as good as another?

tolerated.line: Does that choice actually matter, or is one byte order as good as another?

lines.text: It matters completely.
The same bytes, read the wrong way, hand back a genuinely different value.
Run it for real: those raw bytes, read back in the chosen order, give the exact original value.
Read in the opposite order, the very same bytes give back a different value entirely.
Now turn to the documentation this whole page design is modeled on. It describes exactly what the very first field of its own page header is there to track.
What does it say that first field actually tracks?
The most recent log entry touching that page.
The header ties every page straight back to the log that describes it.
In the documentation's own words: that first field tracks the most recent log entry related to the page, and right beside it sits the page's own checksum, whenever checksums are turned on.
That same documentation says something stronger still, about the little index that points at an item inside a page.
That index is never moved until the item it points to is freed, so it keeps working as a long-term reference, even while the item itself gets shuffled around to make room.

So, pulling this topic together: a page's own checksum genuinely catches a corrupted byte anywhere in its body, but that checksum alone can't catch a deliberate, consistent change to the format; only checking the magic number does.
A page's own byte order has to be explicit and enforced, never assumed.
And the documentation this design is modeled on describes exactly that: a header that tracks its own log position, and an index that lets an item's identity outlive the item being moved.
